intro.speaker: sam
intro.text: Hi! This MapReduce paper is new territory for me and my notes from the first read are honestly a mess.

intro.speaker: sam
intro.text: Can we go unit by unit so I can check I actually understood the model?

L1U1.speaker: sam
L1U1.text: I think Map is the one that merges values together and Reduce just splits the input apart... is that backwards?

L1U2.speaker: sam
L1U2.text: I assumed every example's reduce step does the same kind of work, like adding things up. Let's check that.

L1U3.speaker: sam
L1U3.text: I figured the reduce workers start reading data before the map workers even finish buffering it. Is that right?

L1U4.speaker: sam
L1U4.text: For word count, I was going to have Map just copy each document through, and let Reduce do all the counting. Sound okay?

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: spot the wrong note among Sam's claims about the MapReduce model.

item.speaker: sam
item.prompt: Sam's notes. One line is wrong - show Sam the passage that proves it.

statements.text: Map takes an input pair and produces a set of intermediate key/value pairs.
statements.why: Correct, this is exactly how the Map function is defined.

sourceRefs.quote: Map, written by the user, takes an input pair and pro- duces a set of intermediate key/value pairs.

statements.text: In the word-count example, the reduce function sums all the counts emitted for a particular word.
statements.why: Correct, this is stated directly in the word-count walkthrough.

sourceRefs.quote: The reduce function sums together all counts emitted for a particular word.

statements.text: In Distributed Grep, the reduce step adds together all the matching lines, the same way the URL-counting example totals things up.
statements.why: Grep's reduce step is actually an identity function that just copies matching lines through; it doesn't aggregate or total anything like the URL-counting example does.

sourceRefs.quote: The reduce function is an identity function that just copies the supplied intermedi- ate data to the output.

statements.text: The master only assigns map or reduce tasks to workers after the input has already been split into pieces.
statements.why: Correct, splitting the input and starting up the program copies happens first, then the master assigns tasks to idle workers.

sourceRefs.quote: The master picks idle workers and assigns each one a map task or a reduce task.

hints: One note mixes up the identity-style reduce from one example with the aggregating reduce from another.

outro.speaker: sam
outro.text: Oh wow, I really had grep's reduce step confused with the aggregating ones. Thanks for catching that!

intro.speaker: sam
intro.text: Back again! I read the performance section and the real-world uses, but my notes from that part are shakier than ever.

intro.speaker: sam
intro.text: Can we check them together before I trust any of these numbers?

L3U1.speaker: sam
L3U1.text: I noted that once the transfer rate for the grep job hit zero, the whole job was basically done. That tracks, right?

L3U2.speaker: sam
L3U2.text: I lumped machine learning in with the web/query-mining uses like Zeitgeist. Was that the right bucket?

L3U3.speaker: sam
L3U3.text: If one worker's disk is failing near the end of a sort job, I figured the whole thing just has to wait for it to finish. Right?

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: spot the wrong note among Sam's claims about performance and real-world use.

item.speaker: sam
item.prompt: Sam's notes. One line is wrong - show Sam the passage that proves it.

statements.text: Google's sort run, including startup overhead, finished in 891 seconds, beating the best reported TeraSort benchmark of 1057 seconds.
statements.why: Correct, the paper reports the sort run at 891 seconds compared against the 1057-second TeraSort result.

sourceRefs.quote: Including startup overhead, the entire computation takes 891 seconds.

statements.text: The grep-like computation was essentially finished once its transfer rate hit zero around 80 seconds in.
statements.why: The rate hitting zero only marks the end of map work; the entire computation, including startup overhead, actually takes about 150 seconds.

sourceRefs.quote: The entire computation takes approximately 150 seconds from start to finish.

statements.text: When a job is close to completion, the master schedules backup executions of the remaining in-progress tasks to deal with stragglers.
statements.why: Correct, this is exactly the backup-task mechanism described for handling stragglers.

sourceRefs.quote: the master schedules backup executions of the remaining in-progress tasks.

statements.text: Large-scale machine learning problems and large-scale graph computations are general computing techniques, separate from web/query mining uses like Zeitgeist reports.
statements.why: Correct, these are listed as distinct domains among Google's uses of MapReduce.

hints: One note treats a milestone during the grep job as if it were the end of the whole computation.

outro.speaker: sam
outro.text: Good thing we checked - I was about to swear the grep job ended at 80 seconds, not 150!

outro.speaker: sam
outro.text: Thanks for walking through all of this with me.
